title: JOSEPH NAMED HIS SON “GOD MADE ME FORGET”
paragraphs:
JOSEPH NAMED HIS SON “GOD MADE ME FORGET”
The Pain That Almost Defined Him, The Grace That Rewrote Everything
There are wounds so deep that even years later, a single memory can make your chest tighten.

A name.
A place.
A betrayal.
A face you trusted.
Most people never truly forget what happened to them.

They learn to function.
They learn to smile.
They learn to survive.
But deep inside, the wound remains.
That is why one of the most powerful names in Scripture is hidden inside the story of Joseph.
Not because it sounds beautiful.
But because of what it cost him to say it.
Joseph named his firstborn son Manasseh.
The Bible says:
“And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh: For God, said he, hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house.”
— Genesis 41:51 (KJV)
The Hebrew text reads:
וַיִּקְרָא יוֹסֵף אֶת־שֵׁם הַבְּכוֹר מְנַשֶּׁה כִּי־נַשַּׁנִי אֱלֹהִים אֶת־כָּל־עֲמָלִי וְאֵת כָּל־בֵּית אָבִי
Transliterated:
Vayiqra Yosef et-shem habekhor Menasheh, ki nashani Elohim et-kol amali ve'et kol beit avi.
The key word is:
מְנַשֶּׁה (Menasheh)
Derived from the Hebrew root:
נָשָׁה (nashah)
Meaning:

“To forget.”
“To let go.”
“To no longer be controlled by a memory.”
This is one of the most misunderstood verses in the Bible.
Joseph was not saying God erased his memory.
He still remembered the pit.
He remembered the ropes.
He remembered the slave traders.
He remembered the betrayal.
He remembered Potiphar's wife.
He remembered the prison.
He remembered every year of waiting.
The Hebrew idea is not amnesia.
It is freedom.
Joseph was saying:
“The pain no longer rules me.”
That changes everything.
Because many people reading this know exactly what it feels like to be trapped by yesterday.
You still replay conversations that happened years ago.
You still hear words spoken over you as a child.
You still carry rejection from people who have already moved on.
You still revisit moments that broke your heart.
And maybe nobody knows.

Maybe you worship.
Maybe you serve.
Maybe you smile.
But secretly, the memory still owns part of you.
Joseph understood that struggle.
Before he became Egypt's governor, Joseph was a victim.
Before he wore royal garments, he wore chains.
Before he interpreted dreams, he lived a nightmare.
His own brothers stripped him.
His own brothers sold him.
His own brothers convinced their father he was dead.
Imagine being seventeen years old and realizing the people who should have protected you were the very people who destroyed your life.
That kind of pain leaves scars.
Yet years later, standing in a palace, Joseph looked at his son and chose a name that declared God's victory over his suffering.
Not because the suffering never happened.
But because God's grace had become greater than the suffering.
That is the entire Gospel.
The world says healing means the bad thing never happened.
Scripture says healing means God becomes bigger than what happened.
Joseph's story was never really about Joseph.
It was always pointing toward Jesus.
Because centuries later another beloved Son would be betrayed.
Another innocent Son would be sold for silver.
Another righteous Son would be falsely accused.
Another suffering Son would descend into darkness.
Another Son would emerge victorious.
Joseph was a shadow.
Jesus is the substance.
Joseph was rejected by his brothers.
Jesus came unto His own, and His own received Him not (John 1:11).
Joseph suffered though innocent.
Jesus was completely sinless.
Joseph saved Egypt from famine.
Jesus saves humanity from eternal death.
Joseph forgave those who betrayed him.
Jesus prayed:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.”
— Luke 23:34
In Greek:
Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς· οὐ γὰρ οἴδασιν τί ποιοῦσιν
Transliterated:
Pater, aphes autois; ou gar oidasin ti poiousin.
Even while bleeding, Jesus was extending mercy.
That is grace.
And grace is what transformed Joseph.
The miracle was not that Joseph became powerful.
The miracle was that Joseph did not become bitter.
Power without healing creates tyrants.
Pain without grace creates bitterness.
But pain surrendered to God creates redemption.
Years later, when Joseph finally stood face-to-face with the brothers who sold him, he could have destroyed them.
Nobody would have stopped him.
Nobody would have questioned him.
Nobody would have blamed him.
Yet Joseph chose forgiveness.
Why?
Because God had already healed what they broke.
Some of the most dangerous prisons in the world do not have bars.
They are made of resentment.
Many people are still imprisoned by people who are no longer present.
Joseph refused to live there.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
What if the greatest miracle God wants to perform in your life is not changing your circumstances?
What if it is changing your heart?
What if God is not merely trying to get you out of your pit?
What if He is trying to get the pit out of you?
That is what happened to Joseph.
God did not waste the betrayal.
God did not waste the waiting.
God did not waste the tears.
God did not waste the years.
Every wound became part of a larger story.
When Joseph finally revealed himself to his brothers, he made one of the most profound statements in Scripture:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.”
— Genesis 50:20
The Hebrew text contains a breathtaking contrast.
Human intentions were evil.
God's intentions were good.
The same event.
The same circumstances.
The same betrayal.
Yet God was writing a different ending.
That is the message of the Gospel.
The cross looked like defeat.
It became victory.
The tomb looked final.
It became the beginning.
Sin looked unstoppable.
Grace proved greater.
This is why our ministry theme is not merely a slogan.
It is biblical reality.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
The scandal of Joseph's betrayal became the grace of national salvation.
The scandal of David's failures became the grace of repentance.
The scandal of Peter's denial became the grace of restoration.
The scandal of Saul's persecution became the grace of Paul's ministry.
The scandal of the cross became the grace of redemption.
And perhaps the scandal of your story is not the end either.
Maybe God is still writing.
Maybe the chapter you hate is preparing the testimony that will save someone else's life.
Maybe the wound you are ashamed of will one day become evidence of God's healing power.
Maybe the tears you cry today will become the reason somebody believes tomorrow.
Maybe your Manasseh moment is coming.
Maybe one day you will look back and say:
"It still happened."
"It still hurt."
"But it no longer owns me."
That is not forgetting.
That is redemption.
If this message reached a place in your heart that you rarely allow others to see, be honest.
"Christ is still healing me."
Let your testimony encourage someone who feels alone.
You may never know how desperately they needed this reminder today.
Return to it whenever you need to remember that Jesus specializes in rewriting impossible stories.
If you desire to glorify God through helping spread biblical truth, one practical way is to support and share this ministry.
The same God who turned a pit into a palace can turn your deepest wound into a testimony.
The same Jesus who conquered the grave can conquer the thing you thought would define you forever.
And one day, because of His grace, you may discover that the very thing meant to destroy you became the place where God revealed His glory most clearly.
The memory may remain.
But the chains do not have to.
Because the God who carried Joseph through betrayal, slavery, false accusation, and imprisonment is still carrying His people today.
And He has never failed to finish what He starts.
The wound may explain part of your story.
But it does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
And that changes everything.
The pain remembered is not nearly as powerful as the grace that redeemed it.
